Here Is What The Trailing P/E Misses About Constellation Energy Stock
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Constellation Energy (CEG) stock costs 33.1 times its adjusted earnings for the four quarters to June 2026. This metric is the most frequently quoted P/E ratio and a steep price for one year of profit, although one quarter’s profit was non-operating. That year proved uneven. Constellation reported a $513 million profit on a $47 million operating loss in fiscal Q2 2026. A trailing P/E only looks backward, however, and the price looks different two years out. What does the same price look like on the profit Constellation is expected to earn in fiscal 2026 and 2027?

Based on the consensus forecast, Constellation stock costs 23.1 times its expected fiscal 2026 earnings and 21.0 times its expected fiscal 2027 earnings. Those multiples compare to 33.1 times on the past four quarters.

Those forward prices hold only if the profit arrives. The consensus forecast puts net income at $3,829 million for fiscal 2026. That forecast follows management’s adjusted measure, so it does not compare directly with the $2,319 million Constellation reported for fiscal 2025. Constellation already reported $3,465 million of net income in the four quarters to June 2026, but the 33.1 times multiple uses $2,672 million of adjusted earnings.

For fiscal 2027, the consensus forecast has Constellation’s sales rising 2.8% and its net income rising 10.2%, meaning the company has to earn more on each sale. That expectation puts the forecast net margin at 12.2% for fiscal 2027, compared to 11.4% for fiscal 2026. Constellation’s reported net margin for fiscal 2025 was 9.1%, but that is a reported figure, while the forecast follows management’s adjusted measure.

The forecast’s sales growth for fiscal 2027 is far below the 26.0% Constellation delivered over the four quarters to June 2026. During that period, management credited the acquired company Calpine with part of the rise in fiscal Q2 2026 adjusted operating earnings. Calpine’s sales also count in the 26.0% growth after the deal closed, so part of that gap comes from the acquisition.
The fiscal 2026 forecast sits close to management’s own view.

How Are Big Tech Nuclear Deals Reshaping Growth at Constellation Energy (NASDAQ:CEG)?
sum: Nuclear power leader Constellation Energy (NASDAQ:CEG) Utilities Constellation Energy Corp (NASDAQ:CEG) 257.25 USD -5.130 1.955% Last Updated at: 2026-11-02T21:04:00Z has signed a series of long-term agreements with major technology companies that are reshaping its growth plans. The largest U.S. nuclear operator agreed with Google to fund upgrades at its existing reactors and to supply power from its fleet, shortly after signing a separate deal with Amazon. For readers following Energy Stocks, Constellation sits at the center of the race to power AI data centers with carbon-free electricity.

Under a long-term power purchase agreement, Google will serve as the anchor customer for uprates at Constellation nuclear units in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. Uprates are upgrades to turbines, steam generators and digital control systems that increase how much power existing reactors can produce. Constellation said the agreement supports billions of dollars of new investment, with the first uprate expected in the coming years and the full added capacity delivered early next decade.

The companies also signed a separate long-term energy supply agreement covering a large amount of existing generation from Constellation's fleet in the PJM region. In addition, they formed a multi-year technology alliance under which Constellation will deploy Google Cloud and Gemini tools in its operations.

About a week before the Google announcement, Constellation signed a long-term agreement with Amazon covering power from its Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Maryland, including an uprate expected to come online later this decade. The deal supports billions of dollars of investment at the plant and helps support its license renewal for another two decades.

Building new nuclear plants takes many years and faces high costs and regulatory hurdles. Uprates add capacity at reactors that already exist, avoiding the long timelines and grid connection bottlenecks of new construction. That makes them one of the fastest ways to add firm, carbon-free power to the grid.
For technology companies, uprates offer a way to support new supply rather than simply purchasing existing power that other customers would otherwise use.

Is Constellation Energy Stock’s Drop A Chance To Buy?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Bulls may be betting on Constellation Energy (CEG) selling its nuclear power years ahead to large companies under long-term contracts. You may still view Constellation as a power producer whose profit swings from quarter to quarter. Long-term agreements change one part of that picture by securing buyers for years. Yet the stock lost 34.3% over the past year, while the S&P 500 returned 11.3%. That is the contradiction. So how much of its nuclear power has Constellation already sold ahead?

Management said on the August 6, 2026 call that long-term agreements now cover roughly 30% of Constellation’s clean baseload output, the steady power its nuclear plants produce around the clock. The company has signed approximately 920 megawatts of long-term nuclear deals since the previous call. These contracts run 18.5 years on average, and the buyers are investment-grade customers, companies with strong credit.

Contract signing continued after the call. Constellation and Amazon announced a 20-year agreement on September 30, 2026, adding about 190 megawatts of nuclear capacity at Calvert Cliffs, Maryland’s only nuclear plant. So the Amazon deal does more than sell existing output: it also expands the plant behind it. A larger deal followed on October 6, 2026, when Google signed a 20-year agreement for 890 megawatts of new nuclear capacity from upgrades at 11 Constellation reactors.

Management itself raised the main doubt. Management said in March 2026 that Constellation was behind its targeted timeline for long-term agreements because of new uncertainty in the regulatory environment. By the August call, management said clearer rules from PJM, the grid operator that covers most of Constellation’s business, were fueling a resumption of contracting activity.

The new deals also come with investment in the plants. The company said the Amazon agreement will enable more than $3 billion of infrastructure investment in Maryland. Constellation is also working on financing for more output. On October 27, 2026, it announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $5 billion from the U.S. Department of Energy to raise output at select nuclear plants.

Is This Number The Biggest Risk To Constellation Energy Stock?
sum: Anyone analyzing Constellation Energy (CEG) should look at its debt load first. The company owed $24.7 billion at the end of June 2026. That is nearly three times the $8.3 billion it owed a year earlier. Over the past year to October 16, the stock lost 32.4%, compared with a 16.2% return for the S&P 500. So how heavy is that debt for a company of Constellation’s size?

Constellation’s debt equals 25.3% of its market value, against 20.0% for the S&P 500 treated as a single company. On that measure, the gap is mild. The more significant shift emerges when comparing the company against its own past. Debt stood at $9.1 billion at the end of June 2024 and had edged down a year later. The entire jump came within the last twelve months.

Against that debt, Constellation held $697 million of cash and short-term investments at the end of June 2026. A holder now owns a business carrying a significantly larger debt load than it did a year ago, even though its debt remains only somewhat above the S&P 500’s relative to market value.

Not yet, once investment is counted. Constellation’s free cash flow, the cash left after investment, was below zero in each of the last three quarters. That includes a shortfall of $850 million in the quarter ended March 2026. Management continued to buy back stock over those months. Executives stated on the August 6, 2026 call that the company had spent about $2.2 billion on repurchases so far in 2026.

Real evidence exists on the other side of the ledger. Cash from operations reached $4.2 billion over the twelve months to June 2026, up from $456 million a year earlier. items.t: Alphabet's Constellation Energy (NASDAQ: CEG) Deal Sends Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale (NYSE: SMR) Shares Soaring Despite No Direct Involvement
sum: Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL), the parent company of Google, has agreed to purchase nuclear-generated electricity from Constellation Energy (NASDAQ: CEG) under a landmark 15-year supply contract covering the utility’s existing nuclear power plants.

The agreement also includes a separate 20-year deal for Constellation to supply 890 megawatts of power from new nuclear facilities it will construct specifically to meet Alphabet’s future energy demands.

The long-term commitment from one of the world’s largest technology companies gives Constellation the financial confidence to invest $4.3 billion into new nuclear energy capacity, expanding an already substantial nuclear power portfolio.
Constellation shares rose sharply on the announcement, as investors responded to the scale and duration of the commitment from such a high-profile corporate buyer.

What caught many market watchers off guard, however, was the simultaneous rally in shares of small modular reactor developers Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale (NYSE: SMR), two companies with no direct involvement in the Constellation-Alphabet agreement.

The surge in those stocks reflects a broader read-through that many investors appear to be drawing from the deal, one centered on the growing institutional acceptance of nuclear power as a serious long-term energy solution.

Unlike Constellation, whose typical nuclear facility is designed to serve hundreds of thousands of utility customers across a regional grid, Oklo and NuScale are pursuing an entirely different model for nuclear energy delivery.

What a 20-Year Deal With Amazon Means for Constellation Energy Stock
sum: Constellation Energy (CEG), the largest nuclear power operator in the United States, has signed a 20-year, 690 MW nuclear power agreement with the largest e-commerce operator in the country, Amazon (AMZN). Not stated explicitly, but the deal will primarily involve servicing the cloud giant's AI computing needs.

Under the terms of the deal, Amazon will invest $3 billion to augment and expand Constellation's Calvert Cliffs nuclear plant in Maryland. Currently operating at a capacity of 1,790 MW, the cash injection of $3 billion is expected to bring another 190 MW of power online between 2030 and 2032, which is to be included in the 690 MW.

The deal also has a retail angle, with Constellation set to supply electricity to support Amazon's operations across the 13-state PJM market. This retail supply arrangement is separate from the 20-year PPA for power generated at Calvert Cliffs, with electricity delivered through the regional grid.

Commenting on the deal, CEO Joe Dominguez said, "Amazon's commitment supports the long-term operation of Calvert Cliffs for generations to come and creates a strong foundation for future investment in both the facility and in advanced nuclear technologies."

Spun off from Exelon (EXC) in 2022, Constellation is primarily an independent power producer and competitive energy supplier. It owns and operates power-generation facilities, sells electricity into wholesale markets, and enters into long-term power-purchase agreements (PPAs) with businesses, utilities, and public-sector customers.

sum: Constellation Energy CEG benefits from an expanding Commercial & Industrial (C&I) customer base as businesses, data centers and other large customers seek reliable, long-term power. The company's competitive advantage lies in its large fleet of reliable, carbon-free nuclear generation, which can meet customers' growing electricity needs while supporting their sustainability goals.

The opportunity is becoming increasingly visible in 2026, with CEG signing 920 megawatts (MW) of long-term nuclear Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with investment-grade customers in the second quarter. The contracts have an average duration of 18.5 years, with operations scheduled to begin between 2029 and 2031, and are expected to ramp up fully by 2032. These agreements enhance long-term revenues and earnings visibility, with CEG expecting nearly 30% of its clean baseload generation to be secured under long-term contracts.

The Walmart agreement further demonstrates the potential of C&I demand. Walmart agreed to purchase about 176 MW of nuclear power, including 30 MW of expanded generation capacity at CEG's Dresden facility. The deal supports Walmart's expansion while enabling CEG to invest more at the plant.

The company's existing generation fleet helps meet rising demand faster while reducing reliance on new power plants and transmission infrastructure. CEG targets more than 20% growth in base EPS from 2026 through 2029, along with long-term, rolling three-year base EPS growth of more than 10%.
Overall, growing C&I demand can strengthen CEG's revenues and earnings visibility while improving generation utilization and supporting sustainable long-term growth.

Expanding C&I demand creates opportunities to secure long-term contracts, improve generation utilization and increase earnings visibility. Rising data-center and commercial loads can also support capacity additions and investment in reliable generation.

The key question now is: What could be the stock's future direction?

While media releases or rumors about a substantial change in a company's business prospects usually make its stock 'trending' and lead to an immediate price change, there are always some fundamental facts that eventually dominate the buy-and-hold decision-making.

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

- PJM, which serves 67 million people across 13 states, warned of potential electricity reliability risks from surging demand and extreme temperatures.
- Constellation Energy is one of the largest power producers in the region.
Shares of Constellation Energy Corp. (CEG) slumped nearly 5% on Wednesday, the steepest drop in a month, after Citi slashed the price target on the energy company by nearly 15%.

Citi lowered the price target on CEG to $297 from $348 and maintained a 'Neutral' rating on the shares, implying about 25% upside. The firm said that it had updated the company's model post the PJM meeting.
CEG stock also fell to an annual low of $228.63 following the revision of the downward target.

The grid operator said that it expects peak electricity demand to reach about 159,563 MW on July 1 and 162,860 MW on July 2. PJM cautioned that certain power plants could face operational constraints due to environmental permits and said the "forecasted demand raises a significant risk of emergency conditions that could jeopardize electric reliability and public safety."

sum: Key Takeaways for Constellation Energy Stock as of June 2026
- Analysts rate Constellation Energy stock 14 buys, 6 outperforms, 3 holds, and 1 sell with a mean target of $360, implying around 39% upside from the current price of $259.
- TIKR’s mid-case model values Constellation Energy at $505 by December 2030, implying around 95% total return, or roughly 16% annualized.
- Constellation Energy stock is undervalued at current levels, with normalized EPS forward growth of 26% implied for fiscal 2027 not yet reflected in the share price.
- Constellation posted Q1 adjusted EPS of $2.74, beating the $2.57 consensus, while reaffirming full-year guidance of $11 to $12 per share.
Constellation Energy Stock Beats EPS but the Real Story Is the Earnings Power Ahead

Constellation Energy stock (CEG) has fallen roughly 19% year to date even as the company just posted one of its strongest quarters on record. The largest U.S. nuclear power operator reported first-quarter adjusted operating earnings of $2.74 per share, beating the $2.57 consensus estimate, while GAAP earnings reached $4.49 per share on a one-time tax benefit.
